images.caption: Figure 2:Overview of CompactSplat.A dual-path encoder first extracts and fuses multi-view and single-view features from sparse inputs, which are then processed by a multi-scale U-Net. Concurrently, the Texture-Aware Partitioner (TAP) evaluates scene complexity based on a user-defined threshold to generate multi-level spatial masks. Guided by these masks, the Hierarchical Pyramid Sampler (HPS) adaptively extracts features across decoder levels. Ultimately, this paradigm allocates sparse samples (S.S.) from low-resolution (L.R.) maps to flat regions, and dense samples (D.S.) from high-resolution (H.R.) maps to texturally complex areas.

Figure 3:Multi-resolution rendering comparison of 3D scenes.We visualize rendered RGB images and depth maps at three scaling factors:×1\times 1(bluebox),×2\times 2(greenbox), and×4\times 4(redbox).
Under higher magnification, structural deficiencies in conventional 3D representations become increasingly apparent.
In the RGB domain, primitive sparsity causes unfilled gaps, manifesting as dark, hollow regions.
Correspondingly, in the depth space (where yellow indicates near and blue indicates distant surfaces), these geometric discontinuities erroneously register as spurious near-field artifacts.
In contrast, CompactSplat’s scale-modulated primitives seamlessly tile the surfaces, yielding watertight geometry and artifact-free renderings across all resolutions.

Figure 4:Quantitative analysis.By modulating the partition thresholdτ\tauat inference time, CompactSplat continuously traverses the Pareto frontier. The model achieves extreme reductions in primitive count (measured in Gaussian per pixel, GPP) with virtually negligible degradation in rendering fidelity.
